title: Butter tarts
summary: Small almond-pastry shells filled with a runny, caramel-like butter filling and a few toasted pecans.
steps: Pulse the almond flour, erythritol, xanthan gum and salt in a food processor. Add the butter and egg and pulse until the dough forms a ball. Chill 15 minutes.
Heat the oven to 165 °C (325 °F). Divide the dough into 12 pieces and press each into a cup of a standard 12-cup muffin tin, up the sides to about 2 cm (3/4 in) high.
Bake the shells 8 minutes, until just set.
Whisk the allulose, melted butter, egg, vanilla and salt until smooth. Sprinkle the pecans into the shells and pour the filling over them, about two-thirds full.
Bake 12–15 minutes, until the filling bubbles and the pastry is golden; the centres should still be slightly runny. Cool 30 minutes in the tin before lifting out with a thin knife.
dairy_free_notes: Dairy-free butter gives a slightly less toffee-like filling, and the shells are a little more crumbly; let them cool fully in the tin.
tips: Allulose darkens quickly; the lower 165 °C oven keeps the filling from scorching before the pastry is done.
Whether butter tarts should hold raisins is a long-running Canadian argument; pecans are the low-carb side of it.

origin.history: Butter tarts are one of the few desserts widely thought of as Canadian. The earliest known printed recipe is usually traced to a 1900 community cookbook from Barrie, Ontario, though home cooks were likely making them before then. They are related to other syrup-and-butter pastries such as the Scottish ecclefechan tart and the American pecan pie.
